Commentary of Surah al-Humazah (Chapter 104)

Tafsir of Surah "al-Humazah": it is Meccan by consensus. It has nine verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker.﴾ (104:1)

The discussion of "al-wayl" (woe) has already been given in more than one place [see vol. 2, p. 7, second edition], and its meaning is disgrace, punishment and destruction. It is also said: it is a valley in Hell. ﴿To every scorner and mocker.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: they are those who go about spreading slander (namimah), who sow discord between loved ones, and who seek out the faults of the innocent. On this view, the two words have the same meaning. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most wicked of the servants of Allah, the Exalted, are those who go about spreading slander, who sow discord between loved ones, and who seek out the faults of the innocent." It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that al-humazah is the qattat (tale-bearer), and al-lumazah is the 'ayyab (one who finds fault).

Abu al-Aliyah, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: al-humazah is the one who backbites and reviles a man to his face, and al-lumazah is the one who backbites him from behind when he is absent. From this is the saying of Hassan:

"I struck you, and you were humbled by the abasement of self,
with a rhyme that blazes like the flame."

[The verse as it appears in his Diwan:

"Covered in shame that clothes you,
kindled, blazing like the flame.

Like the strike of a lion who protects our flank,
mighty in the joints of the ribs, [...]"]

al-Nahhas preferred this view and said: from this is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the alms.﴾ (9:58)

Muqatil said, opposite to this: al-humazah is the one who backbites in absence, and al-lumazah is the one who backbites to the face.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: al-humazah is the one who attacks people (with the tongue), and al-humazah is the one who attacks their lineages.

Ibn Zayd said: al-hamiz is the one who strikes people with his hand and beats them, and al-lumazah is the one who finds fault with them with his tongue and disparages them.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: he strikes with his tongue, and he finds fault with his eyes.

Ibn Kaysan said: al-humazah is the one who harms his companions with foul speech, and al-lumazah is the one who narrows his eyes at his companion, and gestures with his eyes, head and eyebrows.

Murrah said: the two are the same; it is the qattat, the one who attacks a man when he is absent.

Ziyad al-A'jam said:

"You show your affection for me when you meet me, falsely,
but when I am absent, you are the striker, the reviler."

Another said:

"When I meet you, you show scorn while smiling at me,
and when I am absent, you become the striker, the reviler."

Al-shahth: the slave. Al-humazah is a form built to express intensity in this meaning, as one says: "sukhzah" and "dahkah," for one who mocks and laughs at people.

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali and al-A'raj read (humzatan lumzatan) with a sukun on the mim in both. If this is authentically reported from them, then it carries the sense of the passive participle: the one who exposes himself to people so that they strike at him and laugh at him, and so that he drives them to backbiting.

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Abu Wa'il, al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash read: "Woe to the humazah, the lumazah."

The root of hamz is breaking and biting down hard on a thing, from which comes "hamz" of a letter (the glottal stop, hamzah). It is said: "I struck (hamaztu) his head." And: "I struck (hamaztu) the walnut with my palm," meaning I broke it. It was said to a Bedouin: "Do you strike the mouse?" He said: "It is the cat that strikes it." The version in al-Sihah: it was said to a Bedouin, "Do you strike the mouse?" and he said, "The tomcat strikes it." The first version was related by al-Tha'labi, and it indicates that the cat is called "humazah." al-'Ajjaj said:

"And whomever we strike on the head, it is shattered."

It is also said: the root of hamz and lamz is pushing and striking. He lamaza him, yalmizuhu, lamzan: when he struck him and pushed him. Likewise hamaza him: that is, pushed him and struck him. The reciter said:

"And whomever we strike in his might, he falls on his back,
upon his backside, a whirlwind or two."

Al-barka'ah: standing on four limbs. He barka'ahu, so he fell (tabarka'a): that is, he threw him down and he fell on his backside, as said in al-Sihah.

The verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, according to what al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas. He used to find fault with people and disparage them, both to their faces and behind their backs. Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, who used to backbite the Prophet (ﷺ) behind his back and attack him to his face. It is also said: it was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It is also said: concerning Jamil ibn Amir al-Thaqafi [in the manuscripts of the original as it stands. In al-Tabari: "Jamil ibn Amir al-Jumahi." In Ibn Hisham's Sirah (p. 229, European edition) and Ibn al-Athir's Tarikh al-Kamil (vol. 2, p. 66, European edition) and some books of tafsir: "Jamil ibn Mu'ammar al-Jumahi."].

It is also said: the verse is general in its address, without being restricted to any particular person. This is the view of most scholars. Mujahid said: it is not specific to anyone; rather it applies to everyone who has this attribute. Al-Farra' said: it is permissible to mention a general thing while intending a specific one, as when one says, "I will never visit you," and then one says, "Whoever does not visit me, I will not visit him," meaning that same speaker.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 104, verse 2:

﴿Who has gathered wealth and counted it.﴾ That is, he prepared it (زَعَمَ, "he claims") for the calamities of time, like كَرُمَ and أَكْرَمَ (both meaning "to be generous"). It was also said: he counted its number; this was said by al-Suddi. Al-Dahhak said: that is, he prepared his wealth for his heirs among his children. It was also said: that is, he boasted of its number and abundance. The intended meaning is blame for withholding wealth from the path of obedience, as He said: ﴿hinderer of good﴾ [Qaf: 25] and He said: ﴿and gathered and hoarded﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 18]. The reading of the majority is جَمَعَ with the م lightened. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i doubled it (جَمَّعَ) to indicate multiplicity, and Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading because of His saying: ﴿and counted it﴾. Al-Hasan, Nasr ibn 'Asim and Abu al-'Aliyah read جَمَعَ lightened, and (وَعَدَدَهُ) also lightened, so they made the doubling apparent, because its original form is عَدَّهُ, and this is far-fetched, since it was written in the Mushaf with two dals. A similar case has come in poetry, where, when they made the doubling apparent, they lightened it. He said:

Gently, Umamah, you have gone beyond my character... Indeed I am generous to people even if they are stingy.

He meant ضَنُّوا and بَخِلُوا, so he made the doubling apparent, but poetry is a place of necessity. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever lightens (وَعَدَدَهُ) it, it is coordinated with "wealth", meaning "and gathered its number", so it is not a verb with the doubling made apparent, because that is used only in poetry.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 104, verses 3–7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He thinks﴾, meaning he supposes, ﴿that his wealth will make him immortal﴾, meaning it will keep him alive and never let him die. This is said by al-Suddi. ʿIkrimah said: it means it will increase his lifespan. It has also been said: it means it gave him life in the past, and the past tense here carries the meaning of the future. It is said: "So-and-so perished by God, and entered the Fire," meaning he will enter it.

﴿No!﴾ is a rejection of what the disbeliever imagined, meaning he will not live forever and his wealth will not last for him. The discussion of "kalla" (no, indeed) has already been treated fully [see vol. 11, p. 147]. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allah, the mawla of Ghufrah, said: "When you hear God, Mighty and Majestic, say ﴿kalla﴾, He is saying, 'You have lied.'"

﴿He will surely be thrown﴾, meaning he will surely be cast down and hurled. Al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Mujahid, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read it as "layunbadhani" in the dual, meaning he and his wealth. Also from al-Hasan: "layunbadhanna" (with a doubled ending, in the singular), meaning his wealth will be thrown. And also from him: "lananbidhannahu" (in the first-person plural), as God's report about Himself, that He throws the owner of the wealth. Also from him: "layunbadhunna" with a dammah on the dhal, on the basis that what is meant is the backbiter, the slanderer, and the wealth that he gathered.

﴿Into the Crusher﴾. It is the Fire of God. It was so named because it breaks everything cast into it, smashes it and crushes it to pieces. The rajiz (the poet) said:

"We smashed Musʿab with the staff,
on the day we broke his nose, to make him angry."

It is the sixth tier of Hell. This is related by al-Mawardi from al-Kalbi. Al-Qushayri related from him that it is the second level (daraka) of the levels of the Fire. al-Dahhak said: it is the fourth level. Ibn Zayd said: it is one of the names of Hell.

﴿And what will make you know what the Crusher is?﴾ This is for the glorification of its status and the emphasis of its affair.

Then He explained what it is, saying: ﴿It is the Fire of God, kindled﴾, meaning that over which it has been kindled for a thousand years, and a thousand years, and a thousand years, so it is never extinguished. God prepared it for the rebellious.

﴿That which rises over the hearts﴾. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: the Fire consumes everything in their bodies, until it reaches the heart. Then they are created anew, and it returns to consuming them. Likewise Khalid ibn Abi ʿImran related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Fire consumes its people until, when it rises over their hearts, it stops. Then when they go forth, it returns, and that is the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿the Fire of God, kindled, that which rises over the hearts﴾." The hearts are singled out because when pain reaches the heart, its owner dies. That is, they are in the state of one who is dying, while they do not die, as God the Exalted said: ﴿He will neither die therein nor live﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74]. So they are, in that case, living in the sense of the dead. It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿rises over the hearts﴾ is that it knows the measure of the punishment each one of them deserves, by the sign that God has preserved to indicate it. It is said: "So-and-so looked upon such-and-such," meaning he knew it. God, the Exalted, has said: ﴿It calls to him who turns his back and withdraws﴾ [al-Maʿarij: 17]. And He said: ﴿When it sees them from a far place, they hear its raging and its roaring﴾ [al-Furqan: 12]. So He described it with this, and it is not far-fetched that it be described as knowing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 104, verse 8–9:

﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾ (8) ﴿in extended columns﴾ (9). I.e., sealed shut (mutbaqah), said al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. The discussion of this has already passed in the commentary on Surah al-Balad [[See p. 72 of this part.]]. It was also said: closed (mughlaqah), in the dialect of Quraysh, who say: "asdtu al-bab" (I closed the door) when one shuts it. This was said by Mujahid. From this is the verse of Ubayd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"Indeed, in the palace, if we entered, a gazelle, its door shut and bolted, the curtain over it."

(﴿in extended columns﴾) The fa' here means the ba': i.e., closed with extended columns. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, and in his recitation it reads "bi-ʿamadin mumaddadah" (with extended columns). And in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Then Allah will send to them angels with enclosures of fire, and nails of fire, and columns of fire, and they will close them over the people of the Fire with those enclosures, and fasten them with those nails, and extend them with those columns, so that no gap remains through which breath can enter, nor any distress exit from it. The Merciful will forget them upon His Throne, and the people of Paradise will be occupied with their bliss, and they will never seek relief after that, and speech will cease, so their speech will be only groaning and sighing. That is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: 'Indeed, it will be closed over them, in extended columns.'"

Qatadah said: "Columns by which they are tormented." This was chosen by al-Tabari. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The extended columns are shackles around their necks." It was also said: fetters on their feet; this was said by Abu Salih. al-Qushayri said: "The majority hold that the columns are the stakes of the enclosures that are closed over the people of the Fire, and those enclosures are fastened with the stakes, so that their distress and heat return upon them, and no relief enters upon them." It was also said: the gates of the Fire are closed over them while they are in columns, i.e., in long chains and shackles, which are firmer and more secure than short ones. It was also said: they are in extended columns, i.e., in its torment and pains, being struck by them. It was also said: the meaning is "in an extended period," i.e., without end.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read (﴿fi ʿumud﴾) with a damma on the ʿayn and the mim: the plural of ʿamud (column). Likewise ʿamad also. Al-Farra' said: "ʿAmad and ʿumud are both sound plurals of ʿamud, like adim, adam, and udum, and afiq, afaq, and ufuq." Abu 'Ubaydah said: ʿamad is the plural of ʿimad, like ihab. Abu 'Ubayd chose ʿamad with two fathas, and so did Abu Hatim, based on the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿He raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 2]. They all agreed on its fatha. al-Jawhari said: "The ʿamud is the pillar of the house; the plural of paucity is a'madah, and the plural of abundance is ʿumud and ʿamad, and both have been read for the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: 'in extended columns.'" Abu 'Ubaydah said: "The ʿamud is every elongated piece of wood or iron, and it is the base of a structure, like the ʿimad. ʿamadtu al-shay'a fa-n'amad," meaning I set the thing up with a support it leans upon. "And a'madtuhu" means I placed a column beneath it.

And Allah knows best.
